issues.legal_issue: An executive may extend a later amendment of an existing law to a union territory under a statutory power to extend laws when the extension supplements, rather than conflicts with or repeals, the law already in force there.
material_facts: The legislature had established a policy of applying the relevant rent legislation in the union territory, and Parliament had extended the principal rent law there.
The challenged notification extended a later amendment that added provisions concerning a subject not covered by the law already extended to the territory.
The Court found that the extended provisions did not conflict with, repeal, or displace the existing law.
issues.conclusion: The notification extending the amendment was valid; the challenge based on excessive delegation and related grounds was rejected.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 87 of the Punjab Reorganisation Act, the Central Government may extend laws in force in a state to Chandigarh, subject to appropriate restrictions or modifications. The power is a form of conditional legislation when it applies an already enacted law to a territory; it is not an unrestricted power to make substantive law. Re Delhi Laws Act, 1912, Ajmer-Merwara (Extension of Laws) Act, 1947 and Part C States (Laws) Act, 1950; R. v. Burah; Ramesh Birch v. Union of India; Vasu Dev Singh v. Union of India; Hamdard Dawakhana v. Union of India; and Hari Shankar Bagla v. State of Madhya Pradesh support the distinction between permissible extension and impermissible repeal or substantive alteration, and the rule that an extension adding provisions may stand alongside existing law if it does not conflict with it.

rule.if: extension_challenge and extension_policy_previously_set and later_rules_add_uncovered_subject and not conflict_with_existing_law

predicates.extension_challenge: A party challenges an executive act extending a later amendment of a law to a territory.
predicates.extension_policy_previously_set: The legislature has established a policy of applying laws from another jurisdiction to the territory by extension.
predicates.later_rules_add_uncovered_subject: The later amendment adds rules about a matter not covered by the law already in force in the territory.
predicates.conflict_with_existing_law: The extended rules repeal, displace, or directly conflict with law already in force in the territory.

issues.definition: When an extension challenge concerns later rules added under an established extension policy, and those rules address an uncovered subject without conflicting with existing law, the extension is valid.

issues.legal_issue: A state legislature may enact rent legislation concerning the landlord-tenant relationship in housing even when the legislation gives a special right to non-resident owners, provided its substance is within the legislature’s assigned field and it does not directly conflict with central legislation.
material_facts: The challenged amendment created a special eviction remedy for certain non-resident owners of residential, scheduled, and non-residential buildings.
The amendment’s dominant purpose was to regulate the relationship between landlords and tenants in relation to housing and accommodation.

Central legislation concerning citizenship, foreign exchange, and the rights of non-residents to own or acquire property addressed different subjects, and the Court found no direct conflict with the rent legislation.
issues.conclusion: The state legislature was competent to enact the amendment, and the Court found no repugnancy between it and the relevant central enactments. For Chandigarh, legislative power over the subject lay with Parliament, and the Central Government could extend the law under the statutory extension power.
issues.legal_principle: Legislative competence is determined by the pith and substance of an enactment and a fair, broad reading of the legislative-list entries. Incidental overlap does not invalidate a law; repugnancy under Article 254 requires a direct and irreconcilable conflict between central and state enactments on substantially the same subject. The Court relied on Entries 17, 18 and 19 of List I; Entry 18 of List II; Entries 6, 7 and 13 of List III; Article 246(4); and Section 87 of the Punjab Reorganisation Act. Indu Bhushan Bose v. Rama Sundari Debi; Jaisingh Jairam Tyagi v. Mamanchand Ratilal Agarwal; V. Dhanapal Chettiar v. Yesodai Ammal; Accountant and Secretarial Services Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India; and Vijay Kumar Sharma v. State of Karnataka informed the analysis of legislative fields, tenancy legislation, and repugnancy.

rule.if: legislative_competence_challenge and dominant_subject_is_housing_tenancy and central_laws_address_distinct_subjects and not direct_irreconcilable_conflict

predicates.legislative_competence_challenge: A party challenges a state enactment as exceeding the state legislature’s lawmaking authority.
predicates.dominant_subject_is_housing_tenancy: The enactment’s main purpose is to regulate landlord-tenant relations concerning housing or accommodation.
predicates.central_laws_address_distinct_subjects: Relevant central enactments regulate subjects distinct from the enactment’s main purpose.
predicates.direct_irreconcilable_conflict: The state and central enactments impose directly incompatible rules on substantially the same subject.

issues.definition: If a competence challenge concerns legislation whose main subject is housing tenancy, and the relevant central laws address distinct subjects without a direct conflict, the state legislation is within competence.

issues.legal_issue: A summary eviction procedure for non-resident owners is not arbitrary or unreasonable where tenants can seek leave to defend on relevant grounds and the procedure preserves review and safeguards against misuse.
material_facts: The tenant may apply for leave to contest by affidavit and must disclose facts that could disentitle the owner from obtaining possession.

The grounds available to the tenant include whether the applicant qualifies as a non-resident owner, owns the building for the required period, and genuinely requires it for personal or dependent use.
The Court held that a tenant need show a strong, well-grounded defence raising triable issues, not establish the defence beyond doubt at the leave stage.

The procedure provides for a High Court review, restricts the owner’s use of the remedy, limits dealings with the recovered property, and provides for restoration or punishment in specified cases of misuse.
issues.conclusion: The summary procedure did not deprive tenants of a legal remedy and was not arbitrary or unreasonable; the constitutional challenge was rejected.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 13-B, 18-A and 19(2-B) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act provide the special remedy, leave-to-defend procedure, review, and safeguards. The claimed need must be genuine and bona fide; a tenant may obtain leave by raising a strong, well-grounded defence on the grounds relevant to eligibility and need, including triable factual disputes. The Court relied on Baldev Singh Bajwa v. Monish Saini; Ravi Dutt Sharma v. Ratan Lal Bhargava; Kewal Singh v. Smt. Lajwanti; Inderjeet Kaur v. Nirpal Singh; Ram Dass v. Ishwar Chander; Bega Begum v. Abdul Ahad Khan; Surjit Singh Kalra v. Union of India; Shiv Sarup Gupta v. Dr. Mahesh Chand Gupta; and Swami Nath v. Nirmal Singh.

rule.if: tenant_remedy_challenge and summary_eviction_proceeding and tenant_can_seek_leave_to_defend and tenant_can_raise_relevant_triable_defence and review_or_abuse_safeguards_exist

predicates.tenant_remedy_challenge: A party challenges the fairness of a special procedure for eviction by a defined class of landlords.
predicates.summary_eviction_proceeding: The challenged proceeding is a summary eviction process for a defined class of landlords.
predicates.tenant_can_seek_leave_to_defend: The tenant may ask to contest the eviction claim by presenting grounds in an affidavit.
predicates.tenant_can_raise_relevant_triable_defenc: The tenant may obtain a hearing by raising a well-grounded factual defence relevant to the landlord’s eligibility or genuine need.
predicates.review_or_abuse_safeguards_exist: The process allows judicial review or provides safeguards against an owner’s misuse of the eviction remedy.

issues.definition: A summary eviction procedure is not arbitrary or unreasonable when tenants can seek leave on relevant triable grounds and review or safeguards exist.

issues.legal_issue: Giving non-resident owners a special summary eviction remedy does not violate equal protection when the class is based on an intelligible distinction connected to a legitimate housing need and the remedy is limited by safeguards.
material_facts: The legislature created a special category of non-resident owners who return to India and require their property for their own use or for the use of a dependent ordinarily living with them.
The stated legislative purpose was to address returning owners’ difficulty in recovering their property under ordinary rent procedures.
The special remedy was limited by requirements concerning ownership, genuine need, the number of times and properties for which it could be used, and restrictions after recovery of possession.
Tenants retained the opportunity to challenge the owner’s eligibility and the genuineness of the claimed need.
issues.conclusion: The classification of non-resident owners was not arbitrary and did not violate Article 14; the challenge was rejected.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 permits a classification founded on intelligible differentia that has a rational nexus to the object of the law. The assessment is practical and considers the purpose of the law and the circumstances that prompted it; a classification need not be perfect, and legislative choices receive a presumption of constitutionality unless palpably arbitrary. The Court relied on Ram Krishna Dalmia v. Justice S.R. Tendolkar; State of A.P. v. Nallamilli Rami Reddi; Kewal Singh v. Smt. Lajwanti; and Ravi Dutt Sharma v. Ratan Lal Bhargava, and considered the need to balance landlord and tenant interests discussed in Malpe Vishwanath Acharya v. State of Maharashtra, Joginder Pal v. Naval Kishore Behal, Satyawati Sharma v. Union of India, and Vinod Kumar v. Ashok Kumar Gandhi.

rule.if: equal_protection_challenge and distinct_returning_owner_class and special_remedy_has_rational_connection_to_rehousing_need and genuine_need_is_required and tenant_can_challenge_claim and misuse_safeguards_exist

predicates.equal_protection_challenge: A party argues that a law’s differential treatment of a defined group violates equal protection.
predicates.distinct_returning_owner_class: The law groups owners who live abroad and return to require their property for themselves or a dependent.
predicates.special_remedy_has_rational_connection_t: The special procedure addresses the group’s identified difficulty in recovering property needed for personal use after return.
predicates.genuine_need_is_required: The owner must establish a genuine need for the property.
predicates.tenant_can_challenge_claim: The tenant may contest the owner’s eligibility or asserted need.
predicates.misuse_safeguards_exist: The law restricts repeated use of the remedy or imposes controls on the owner after possession is recovered.

issues.definition: A special classification is constitutionally valid when it distinguishes returning owners in a way rationally connected to their rehousing need and requires genuine need while allowing tenant challenges and guarding against misuse.
